summary: A joke RFC published on April 1 that pretends to define a Telnet option for displaying subliminal messages. It is humor and not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke document that pretends to hide secret messages in a chat tool. It was written as an April Fools prank.

questions: how to send hidden messages in telnet
subtitle: An April Fools' joke about hiding secret messages in Telnet sessions.

tldr.problem: Users stubbornly continue using outdated versions of Telnet despite announcements and newsletters encouraging them to upgrade.
tldr.mechanism: This April 1st joke proposes a SUBLIMINAL-MESSAGE Telnet option (code 257) that flashes hidden messages on the user's terminal at specified intervals and durations, using unused Telnet command bits and a subnegotiation format with parameters for message duration and display frequency.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is pure humor; no actual Telnet implementation includes subliminal messages. The joke playfully suggests coercive persuasion as a response to user resistance to upgrades.

today: RFC 1097 is a historic April Fools' RFC and remains pure humor. No Telnet implementation includes the SUBLIMINAL-MESSAGE option, and the practice of sending subliminal messages would be universally considered unethical and likely illegal. The RFC has become a beloved example of the Internet community's tradition of publishing jokes on April 1st, with RFC 854 (the Telnet specification) serving as the real reference for how Telnet options actually work.

sections.title: The Upgrade Problem
sections.content: This is an April 1st joke document. RFC 1097 is written as if it were a serious protocol specification, but it is pure humor, not a real standard. The RFC frames the problem humorously: users resist upgrading to newer versions of Telnet, continuing to use outdated software for years despite banners and newsletters. The author encountered this problem at CMU and notes that gentler persuasion had failed. The solution, presented tongue-in-cheek, is to use Telnet to display subliminal messages that the conscious mind does not notice but the brain supposedly absorbs, motivating users to upgrade.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a joke. It says: "People won't upgrade to the new Telnet. What if we showed them secret messages so fast they don't notice, but their brains do?" It is silly.

sections.title: The SUBLIMINAL-MESSAGE Option
sections.content:
The RFC defines a SUBLIMINAL-MESSAGE Telnet option with code 257, following standard Telnet negotiation. The sender uses the WILL, WONT, DO, and DONT commands to negotiate whether subliminal messages are enabled. The actual message is sent via subnegotiation: a 16-bit duration (in milliseconds), a 16-bit frequency (in seconds between displays), and a message string.

The RFC includes implementation notes suggesting that the client's ability to erase messages quickly depends on terminal capabilities and phosphor persistence. CMU's implementation takes into account line speed and terminal capabilities. A version under development at the time even proposed displaying messages using Morse code on the keyboard caps-lock LED.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke defines pretend commands to turn subliminal messages on or off, and how to send them: how long to show them, how often to show them, and what message to show.

sections.title: Subliminal Persuasion in Action
sections.content:
The RFC includes three examples. In the first, a server sends the message "Use VMS" repeatedly, which the author jokingly notes is "a stable operating system, not an unreasonable request." In the second, the server replaces one message with another ("Go home"). In the third, the server sends an empty message to stop all subliminal messaging.

The RFC concludes with a playful acknowledgment from CMU that "we do things just a little sneakier here at CMU," cementing the humorous intent.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how a server could flash "Use VMS" at you over and over, or change what message it is showing, or stop showing messages.

references.text: Postel, J. and J. Reynolds, "Telnet Protocol Specification", STD 8, RFC 854, May 1983.
